title: 13. Scaling to Millions: Caching, Message Queues & Real-Time Communication
summary: Covers The Secret Weapons Behind Every Fast Application, Caching, Caching Strategies, Message Queues, Celery and more.
objectives: The Secret Weapons Behind Every Fast Application

sections.title: 1. Caching
sections.body:
### Why Cache? (The Speed Difference)

```
Without Cache:
  User requests product page
  → Server queries PostgreSQL (50-200ms)
  → Build response (10ms)
  → Total: 60-210ms per request

  1000 concurrent users = 1000 DB queries = DB OVERLOADED!

With Cache (Redis):
  First request:
    → Check Redis (1ms) → MISS → Query PostgreSQL (100ms) → Store in Redis → Return

  Next 999 requests:
    → Check Redis (1ms) → HIT → Return cached data
    → Total: 1-2ms per request ⚡
    → Database is barely touched!
```

### Redis Basics

```
Redis = In-Memory Key-Value Store
  ├── Data lives in RAM (not disk) → Blazing fast
  ├── Think of it as a super-fast dictionary/hashmap
  ├── Supports: Strings, Lists, Sets, Hashes, Sorted Sets
  └── Used by: Twitter, GitHub, Snapchat, ChatGPT

Speed comparison:
  PostgreSQL query: 10-100ms
  Redis GET:        0.1-1ms (100x faster!)
```

### Redis with FastAPI

```python
import redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
import json

app = FastAPI()
redis_client = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379", decode_responses=True)

# ─── Basic Cache Pattern ───
@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
async def get_product(product_id: int):
    # 1. Try cache first
    cache_key = f"product:{product_id}"
    cached = await redis_client.get(cache_key)

    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)  # Cache HIT — return instantly!

    # 2. Cache MISS — query database
    product = await db.get_product(product_id)

    # 3. Store in cache for next time (expire in 5 minutes)
    await redis_client.setex(cache_key, 300, json.dumps(product))

    return product

# ─── Cache Invalidation (When Data Changes) ───
@app.put("/products/{product_id}")
async def update_product(product_id: int, data: ProductUpdate):
    # 1. Update in database
    product = await db.update_product(product_id, data)

    # 2. Delete old cache (next read will re-cache)
    await redis_client.delete(f"product:{product_id}")

    # 3. Also invalidate list caches
    await redis_client.delete("products:list:page:1")

    return product
```

sections.title: 2. Caching Strategies
sections.body:
### Strategy 1: Cache-Aside (Most Common)

```
Application manages the cache:

  READ:
    1. Check cache → If HIT → return
    2. If MISS → Query DB → Store in cache → return

  WRITE:
    1. Write to DB
    2. Invalidate (delete) cache
```

### Strategy 2: Write-Through Cache

```
Every write goes to BOTH cache and DB:

  WRITE:
    1. Write to cache
    2. Cache writes to DB (synchronously)

  READ:
    1. Always read from cache (always up-to-date)

  ✅ Cache is always consistent
  ❌ Writes are slower (double write)
```

### Strategy 3: Write-Behind (Write-Back)

```
Write to cache first, DB later (async):

  WRITE:
    1. Write to cache (instant!)
    2. Cache batches writes to DB every N seconds

  ✅ Super fast writes
  ❌ Risk of data loss if cache crashes
  Use for: Analytics, view counts, "likes"
```

### What to Cache and What NOT to Cache

```
✅ CACHE THESE:
  ├── Database query results (product listings, user profiles)
  ├── API responses from external services
  ├── Computed results (analytics, recommendations)
  ├── Session data
  ├── Rate limiting counters
  └── Configuration/feature flags

❌ DON'T CACHE THESE:
  ├── Frequently changing data (stock prices, live scores)
  ├── User-specific sensitive data
  ├── Large binary data (use CDN instead)
  └── Data that MUST be real-time accurate
```

### Redis for Rate Limiting

```python
async def rate_limit_check(user_id: str, max_requests: int = 100, window: int = 3600):
    """Sliding window rate limiter using Redis"""
    key = f"rate_limit:{user_id}"
    now = time.time()

    pipe = redis_client.pipeline()

    # Remove old entries outside the window
    pipe.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, now - window)
    # Add current request
    pipe.zadd(key, {str(now): now})
    # Count requests in window
    pipe.zcard(key)
    # Set expiry on the key
    pipe.expire(key, window)

    results = await pipe.execute()
    request_count = results[2]

    if request_count > max_requests:
        raise HTTPException(429, "Rate limit exceeded")

    return request_count

# How ChatGPT/Claude rate limits work:
# Free tier:  25 messages per 3 hours  → rate_limit("user_1", 25, 10800)
# Plus tier:  100 messages per 3 hours → rate_limit("user_1", 100, 10800)
# API tier:   Based on tokens/minute   → rate_limit("api_key_1", 60, 60)
```

### Redis for Session Storage

```python
import uuid

class SessionManager:
    def __init__(self, redis_client, expire_seconds=86400):
        self.redis = redis_client
        self.expire = expire_seconds

    async def create_session(self, user_data: dict) -> str:
        session_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        await self.redis.setex(
            f"session:{session_id}",
            self.expire,
            json.dumps(user_data)
        )
        return session_id

    async def get_session(self, session_id: str) -> dict | None:
        data = await self.redis.get(f"session:{session_id}")
        return json.loads(data) if data else None

    async def destroy_session(self, session_id: str):
        await self.redis.delete(f"session:{session_id}")
```

sections.title: 3. Message Queues
sections.body:
### The Problem: Doing Too Much in One Request

```
E-commerce checkout WITHOUT queue:

POST /checkout
  ├── Validate cart (50ms)
  ├── Process payment via Stripe (2000ms)     ← SLOW external API
  ├── Update inventory (100ms)
  ├── Send confirmation email (500ms)          ← SLOW
  ├── Send SMS notification (300ms)            ← SLOW
  ├── Update analytics (100ms)
  └── Generate invoice PDF (800ms)             ← SLOW

  Total: 3.85 seconds!
  User stares at loading spinner for 4 seconds!

POST /checkout WITH queue:
  ├── Validate cart (50ms)
  ├── Process payment via Stripe (2000ms)
  ├── Create order in DB (100ms)
  └── Publish "order.created" event to queue (5ms)

  Total: 2.15 seconds (user sees "Order placed!")

  Meanwhile, in the background:
  ├── Email Worker → Sends confirmation email
  ├── SMS Worker → Sends SMS notification
  ├── Analytics Worker → Updates dashboard
  └── Invoice Worker → Generates PDF
```

### Message Queue Architecture

```
┌──────────┐    publish     ┌──────────────┐    consume     ┌──────────┐
│ Producer │ ──────────────►│ Message Queue │ ──────────────►│ Consumer │
│ (API)    │    message     │ (RabbitMQ/    │    message     │ (Worker) │
│          │                │  Redis/Kafka) │                │          │
└──────────┘                └──────────────┘                └──────────┘

Key Concepts:
  Producer = The code that creates tasks (your API endpoint)
  Queue    = Where tasks wait to be processed
  Consumer = The code that processes tasks (background worker)

  Messages are PERSISTENT — if worker crashes, message stays in queue
  Messages are ACKnowledged — worker confirms when task is done
```

### RabbitMQ vs Redis Queue vs Kafka

```
┌─────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┐
│             │ RabbitMQ       │ Redis (Queue)  │ Apache Kafka   │
├─────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Best For    │ Task queues    │ Simple queues  │ Event streaming│
│ Speed       │ Fast           │ Very fast      │ Very fast      │
│ Durability  │ Persistent     │ Optional       │ Persistent     │
│ Scale       │ Medium         │ Medium         │ Massive        │
│ Complexity  │ Medium         │ Simple         │ Complex        │
│ Use Case    │ Email sending, │ Session queue, │ Log processing,│
│             │ order process  │ cache invalidn │ analytics      │
├─────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Used By     │ Instagram,     │ GitHub,        │ LinkedIn,      │
│             │ Reddit         │ Snapchat       │ Uber, Netflix  │
└─────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┘
```

sections.title: 4. Celery
sections.body:
### Python's Standard Task Queue (Works with RabbitMQ or Redis)

```python
# ─── celery_config.py ───
from celery import Celery

celery_app = Celery(
    "tasks",
    broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",       # Where tasks are queued
    backend="redis://localhost:6379/1",       # Where results are stored
)

celery_app.conf.update(
    task_serializer="json",
    result_serializer="json",
    accept_content=["json"],
    timezone="UTC",
    task_track_started=True,
    task_time_limit=300,         # Kill task after 5 minutes
    worker_max_tasks_per_child=1000,  # Restart worker after 1000 tasks (memory leak prevention)
)

# ─── tasks.py ───
from celery_config import celery_app
import smtplib
from email.mime.text import MIMEText

@celery_app.task(bind=True, max_retries=3)
def send_email_task(self, to_email: str, subject: str, body: str):
    """Background task to send email"""
    try:
        msg = MIMEText(body)
        msg["Subject"] = subject
        msg["To"] = to_email

        with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.gmail.com", 587) as server:
            server.starttls()
            server.login("your-email@gmail.com", "app-password")
            server.send_message(msg)

        return {"status": "sent", "to": to_email}
    except Exception as exc:
        # Retry in 60 seconds
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=60)

@celery_app.task
def generate_invoice_pdf(order_id: int):
    """Background task to generate invoice"""
    order = get_order_from_db(order_id)
    pdf = create_pdf(order)
    upload_to_s3(f"invoices/{order_id}.pdf", pdf)
    return {"status": "generated", "url": f"https://cdn.app.com/invoices/{order_id}.pdf"}

@celery_app.task
def process_ml_prediction(data: dict):
    """Background task for ML inference"""
    model = load_model("recommendation_model")
    predictions = model.predict(data)
    return {"predictions": predictions.tolist()}

# ─── FastAPI integration ───
from fastapi import FastAPI
from tasks import send_email_task, generate_invoice_pdf

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(order: OrderCreate):
    # 1. Create order in DB (fast)
    new_order = await db.create_order(order)

    # 2. Queue background tasks (instant — just adds to queue)
    send_email_task.delay(
        to_email=order.email,
        subject="Order Confirmation",
        body=f"Your order #{new_order.id} has been placed!"
    )
    generate_invoice_pdf.delay(order_id=new_order.id)

    # 3. Return immediately (user doesn't wait for email/PDF)
    return {"order_id": new_order.id, "status": "created"}
```

### Running Celery

```bash
# Start the Celery worker
celery -A celery_config worker --loglevel=info --concurrency=4

# Start Celery Beat (for scheduled tasks)
celery -A celery_config beat --loglevel=info

# Monitor with Flower (web dashboard)
celery -A celery_config flower --port=5555
```

### Scheduled Tasks (Celery Beat)

```python
from celery.schedules import crontab

celery_app.conf.beat_schedule = {
    # Send daily analytics email every morning at 8 AM
    "daily-analytics": {
        "task": "tasks.send_daily_analytics",
        "schedule": crontab(hour=8, minute=0),
    },
    # Clean up expired sessions every hour
    "cleanup-sessions": {
        "task": "tasks.cleanup_expired_sessions",
        "schedule": crontab(minute=0),  # Every hour
    },
    # Generate ML recommendations every 6 hours
    "update-recommendations": {
        "task": "tasks.update_user_recommendations",
        "schedule": timedelta(hours=6),
    },
}
```

sections.title: 5. WebSockets
sections.body:
### How Real-Time Chat Works (WhatsApp, Slack, Discord)

```
HTTP (Request-Response):
  Client: "Any new messages?" → Server: "No"       (0.5s later)
  Client: "Any new messages?" → Server: "No"       (0.5s later)
  Client: "Any new messages?" → Server: "Yes! 1"   (0.5s later)
  Problem: Constant polling = wasted bandwidth!

WebSocket (Persistent Connection):
  Client ←─── always connected ───► Server

  Server pushes message instantly when it arrives
  No polling needed! True real-time!
```

```
HTTP:                          WebSocket:
┌────────┐    ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐    ┌────────┐
│ Client │───►│ Server │      │ Client │◄══►│ Server │
│        │◄───│        │      │        │    │        │
└────────┘    └────────┘      └────────┘    └────────┘
 No message?   No.             Connected! Both can send
 No message?   No.             Server: "New message!"
 No message?   Yes → data      Server: "User typing..."
                                Server: "User online"
```

### FastAPI WebSocket Chat

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect
from typing import Dict, List
import json

app = FastAPI()

class ConnectionManager:
    """Manages all WebSocket connections"""

    def __init__(self):
        # room_id → list of connected WebSockets
        self.rooms: Dict[str, List[WebSocket]] = {}

    async def connect(self, websocket: WebSocket, room_id: str):
        await websocket.accept()
        if room_id not in self.rooms:
            self.rooms[room_id] = []
        self.rooms[room_id].append(websocket)

    def disconnect(self, websocket: WebSocket, room_id: str):
        self.rooms[room_id].remove(websocket)
        if not self.rooms[room_id]:
            del self.rooms[room_id]

    async def broadcast(self, room_id: str, message: dict):
        """Send message to ALL users in a room"""
        for connection in self.rooms.get(room_id, []):
            try:
                await connection.send_json(message)
            except:
                pass

manager = ConnectionManager()

@app.websocket("/ws/chat/{room_id}")
async def websocket_chat(websocket: WebSocket, room_id: str):
    # Authenticate (check JWT token from query params)
    token = websocket.query_params.get("token")
    user = verify_token(token)

    await manager.connect(websocket, room_id)

    # Notify room that user joined
    await manager.broadcast(room_id, {
        "type": "user_joined",
        "user": user.email,
        "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    })

    try:
        while True:
            # Wait for message from this client
            data = await websocket.receive_json()

            # Save to database
            await db.save_message(room_id, user.id, data["content"])

            # Broadcast to all users in room
            await manager.broadcast(room_id, {
                "type": "message",
                "user": user.email,
                "content": data["content"],
                "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
            })

    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(websocket, room_id)
        await manager.broadcast(room_id, {
            "type": "user_left",
            "user": user.email
        })
```

diagrams.title: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  Note over C,S: Polling — ask repeatedly
  C->>S: anything new?
  S-->>C: no
  Note over C,S: Server-Sent Events — one long HTTP response
  C->>S: GET /stream
  S-->>C: data chunk 1
  S-->>C: data chunk 2 (LLM tokens, notifications)
  Note over C,S: WebSocket — full duplex
  C->>S: upgrade
  S-->>C: message
  C->>S: message (chat, games, collaboration)
diagrams.explain: **Polling** is simple but wastes requests and adds delay. **SSE** keeps one HTTP response open and streams server-to-client events — the standard way to stream LLM tokens and notifications, with automatic reconnect. **WebSockets** give a two-way channel for chat, multiplayer games and collaborative editing, at the cost of stateful connections the load balancer must handle.

sections.title: 6. SSE
sections.body:
### How ChatGPT Streams Responses (Token by Token)

```
Regular HTTP:
  User: "Explain quantum physics"
  ... waits 10 seconds ...
  Server: "Quantum physics is a branch of physics..." (all at once)

SSE (Server-Sent Events):
  User: "Explain quantum physics"
  Server: "Quantum"
  Server: " physics"
  Server: " is"
  Server: " a"
  Server: " branch"
  Server: " of"
  Server: " physics"
  Server: "..."
  (User sees text appearing word by word — like ChatGPT!)
```

### FastAPI SSE — ChatGPT-Style Streaming

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

async def generate_llm_response(prompt: str):
    """Simulate LLM streaming (replace with actual LLM call)"""
    # In reality: use OpenAI/LangChain streaming
    response = "Quantum physics is a fundamental theory that describes nature at the atomic scale."

    for word in response.split():
        yield f"data: {word} \n\n"  # SSE format
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)     # Simulate token generation delay

    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.get("/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(prompt: str):
    return StreamingResponse(
        generate_llm_response(prompt),
        media_type="text/event-stream"
    )

# ─── Real LangChain Streaming ───
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.callbacks import AsyncIteratorCallbackHandler

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def chat_with_ai(request: ChatRequest):
    callback = AsyncIteratorCallbackHandler()
    llm = ChatOpenAI(
        model="gpt-4",
        streaming=True,
        callbacks=[callback]
    )

    async def generate():
        task = asyncio.create_task(llm.ainvoke(request.message))
        async for token in callback.aiter():
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'token': token})}\n\n"
        await task
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
```
1. CACHE everything you read frequently (Redis)
2. Use CACHE-ASIDE pattern for most use cases
3. INVALIDATE cache when data changes
4. QUEUE slow operations (email, PDF, ML) with Celery
5. Use WEBSOCKETS for real-time features (chat, notifications)
6. Use SSE for streaming responses (like ChatGPT)
7. RATE LIMIT to prevent abuse (Redis sorted sets)
```
